definitions.text: Ungainly; clumsy; awkward; also, troublesome; inconvenient. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Beau. & Pl.
The state or quality of being ungainly; awkwardness.
Not gainly; not expert or dexterous; clumsy; awkward; uncouth; as, an ungainly strut in walking. His ungainly figure and eccentric manners. Macaulay.
Unsuitable; unprofitable. [Obs.] Hammond.
In an ungainly manner.
To strip of gear; to unharness; to throw out of gear.
A person so far out of the protection of the law, that if he were murdered, no geld, or fine, should be paid, or composition made by him that killed him. Cowell. Burrill.
Not generous; illiberal; ignoble; unkind; dishonorable. The victor never will impose on Cato Ungenerous terms. Addison.
In an ungenerous manner.
Destitute of genitals; impotent. [R.] Shak.

Not gentle; lacking good breeding or delicacy; harsh. Vicious, ungentle, foolish, blunt, unkind. Shak. That ungentle flavor which distinguishes nearly all our native and uncultivated grapes. Hawthorne.
To cause to be unbegotten or unborn, or as if unbegotten or unborn. [R.] I 'll disown you, I 'll disinherit you, I 'll unget you. Sheridan.
Being without gifts, especially native gifts or endowments. Cowper.
To loose the girdle or band of; to unbind; to unload. He ungirded his camels. Gen. xxiv. 32.
To yield; to relax; to give way. [Obs.]
The siamang; -- called also ungka ape.
The agile gibbon; -- called also ungka-pati, and ungka-etam. See Gibbon.
To strip of glass; to remove the glazing, or glass, from, as a window.
To deprive of glory. [R.] I. Watts.
Inglorious. [Obs.] Wyclif.
To take off the glove or gloves of; as, to unglove the hand. Beau. & Fl.
To separate, part, or open, as anything fastened with glue. She stretches, gapes, unglues her eyes, And asks if it be time to rise. Swift.
To deprive of divinity; to undeify. [R.] Donne.
To cause to recognize no god; to deprive of a god; to make atheistical. [R.] Dryden.
Not godly; not having regard for God; disobedient to God; wicked; impious; sinful.
Polluted by sin or wickedness. The hours of this ungodly day. Shak.
Not stained with gore; not bloodied. Sylvester.
Not gored or pierced.
Not gotten; not acquired.
Not begotten. [Obs. or Poetic] "His loins yet full of ungot princes." Waller.
Not gotten; not acquired.
Not begotten. [Obs. or Poetic] "His loins yet full of ungot princes." Waller.
Not governable; not capable of being governed, ruled, or restrained; licentious; wild; unbridled; as, ungovernable passions.
To strip of a gown; to unfrock.
Etym: [1 st pref. un- + gown.]
Stripped of a gown; unfrocked.
Etym: [Pref. un- not + gowned.]
Not having, or not wearing, a gown.

Not graceful; not marked with ease and dignity; deficient in beauty and elegance; inelegant; awkward; as, ungraceful manners; ungraceful speech. The other oak remaining a blackened and ungraceful trunk. Sir W. Scott.
Not gracious; showing no grace or kindness; being without good will; unfeeling. Shak.
Having no grace; graceless; wicked. [Obs.] Shak.
Not well received; offensive; unpleasing; unacceptable; not favored. Anything of grace toward the Irish rebels was as ungracious at Oxford as at London. Clarendon.
Displeasing; ungrateful; ingrate. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.
Not grateful; not thankful for favors; making no returns, or making ill return for kindness, attention, etc.; ingrateful. South.
Unpleasing; unacceptable; disagreeable; as, harsh sounds are ungrateful to the ear.
To raise or remove from the grave; to disinter; to untomb; to exhume. [Obs.] Fuller.
Of or pertaining to a nail, claw, talon, or hoof, or resembling one.
Having a nail, claw, or hoof attached; -- said of certain bones of the feet.
To deprive of a guard; to leave unprotected. [R.] Sterne.
Ungual.
A lubricant or salve for sores, burns, or the like; an ointment. Cowper. cerate.
Like an unguent, or partaking of its qualities.
Unguentary.
In a manner not becoming to a guest. [R.] Milton.
Ungual.
Of or pertaining to a claw or a nail; ungual.
An extensive division of Mammalia including those having claws or nails, as distinguished from the hoofed animals (Ungulata).
One of the Unguiculata.
Furnished with nails, claws, or hooks; clawed. See the Note under Nail, n., 1.
(Bot.)
Furnished with a claw, or a narrow stalklike base, as the petals of a carnation.
Furnished with nails, claws, or hooks; clawed. See the Note under Nail, n., 1.
(Bot.)
Furnished with a claw, or a narrow stalklike base, as the petals of a carnation.
Producing, having, or supporting nails or claws.
Having the form of a claw or claws.
Consisting of, or resembling, fat or oil; oily; unctuous; oleaginous.
The nail, claw, talon, or hoof of a finger, toe, or other appendage.
(Zoöl.)
One of the terminal hooks on the foot of an insect.
(Bot.)
The slender base of a petal in some flowers; a claw; called also ungula.
A hoof, claw, or talon.
(Geom.)
A section or part of a cylinder, cone, or other solid of revolution, cut off by a plane oblique to the base; -- so called from its resemblance to the hoof of a horse.
(Bot.)
Same as Unguis, 3. Spherical ungula (Geom.), a part of a sphere bounded by two planes intersecting in a diameter and by a line of the surface of the sphere.
Of or pertaining to a hoof, claw, or talon; ungual.
An extensive group of mammals including all those that have hoofs. It comprises the Artiodactyla and Perissodactyla.
Shaped like a hoof.
(Zoöl.)
Furnished with hoofs. See the Note under Nail, n., 1.
Any hoofed quadruped; one of the Ungulata.
Hoofed, or bearing hoofs; -- used only when these are of a tincture different from the body.
Having, or walking on, hoofs.
Same as Ungulate.
